props.title: Manhattan
props.initialSlug: A neurotic writer's affair with a teenage girl in NYC

sections.content: Manhattan represents Woody Allen's most visually stunning achievement, shot in gorgeous black-and-white by Gordon Willis. The film's 2.35:1 widescreen compositions and Gershwin score create an idealized version of New York that contrasts sharply with the messy romantic entanglements of its characters. Like Annie Hall (1977), it explores Allen's familiar themes of love, relationships, and neurosis, but with a more sophisticated visual palette and deeper emotional resonance. The controversial relationship between Allen's 42-year-old character and Mariel Hemingway's 17-year-old Tracy now reads very differently given later allegations, but the film remains a masterpiece of cinematography and urbane comedy.

sections.content: The film belongs to a golden age of New York movies in the late 1970s, alongside The Warriors (1979), All That Jazz (1979), and Taxi Driver (1976). These films captured the city during a period of decay and reinvention, though Allen's version is deliberately romanticized. The opening montage set to "Rhapsody in Blue" established a template for idealized New York sequences that influenced countless later films, from When Harry Met Sally (1989) to Autumn in New York (2000).

Allen's creative partnership with cinematographer Gordon Willis proved crucial. Willis, known as "The Prince of Darkness" for his work on The Godfather (1972), brought his signature high-contrast style to Manhattan's black-and-white imagery. The film's visual sophistication elevated it above typical romantic comedies, creating an artistic bridge between the European art films Allen admired like 8½ (1963) and accessible American comedy. sections.content: Manhattan's influence extends beyond cinema into how we collectively imagine New York. The film's romantic vision of the city, with its skyline shots and cultural touchstones like the Guggenheim and Central Park, helped cement the idea of New York as a sophisticated cultural capital. Later films like You've Got Mail (1998) and Serendipity (2001) would follow this template, though none matched Manhattan's artistic ambition or visual poetry.
